1099-K RECONCILIATION WORKSHEET · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Why is your 1099-K higher than what you actually made?

Add one row per Form 1099-K you received this year — Etsy, eBay, Poshmark, Mercari, Depop, Whatnot, StockX, or any other marketplace or payment app — with the Box 1a amount it reports, then back out refunds, the sales tax the marketplace collected and remitted for you, and your own costs. See a reconciled estimate per platform and combined across all of them.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer. See why the gap exists for the two-minute explanation of what Box 1a legally represents, or how this compares to reconciling it yourself in a spreadsheet.

Still owe quarterly estimated tax on this income as the year goes? The quarterly estimated tax calendar is the other end of the same tax year — that page sets aside payments as you go, this one reconciles what the marketplace actually reported once the year is over.

Paying someone else on 1099-K income instead — a contractor, freelancer, or vendor of your own? The 1099-NEC vendor tracker flags which of them cross the 2026 $2,000 reporting threshold and whose W-9 is still missing — nothing uploaded there either.

Not sure a 1099-K is coming at all this year? The 1099-K threshold checker estimates whether a platform is likely to issue one, per platform and per tax year, against the federal threshold's four changes since 2022 plus four states' own stricter rule — this page is for the form once you already have it.

What this does and doesn't do

Box 1a of each 1099-K is a gross figure — before refunds, fees, discounts, or any sales tax the marketplace itself collected and remitted for you are backed out, per the IRS's own General Instructions for Forms 1099-K. This worksheet backs those out, then subtracts the costs you enter (fees, cost of goods sold, shipping) to estimate net profit. It does not know about your 1099-NEC, W-2, or other income, does not determine your actual tax liability, and does not file anything. Verify every figure against the platform's own 1099-K and payout statements before relying on it.

Common questions

Why is my 1099-K higher than what I actually made?

Form 1099-K Box 1a reports the gross amount of payment-card and third-party network transactions before any adjustment for refunds, fees, discounts, or credits — that is how the IRS's own instructions for the form define it. Many marketplaces also collect and remit sales tax on your behalf as a "marketplace facilitator," and that tax often passes through the same payout and lands in Box 1a too, even though it was never your money. None of that is your taxable income; this worksheet backs it out.

Do I have to report the full Box 1a amount as income?

No — Box 1a is a gross reporting figure, not a determination of your taxable income. What you actually owe tax on is your net profit: gross receipts (after backing out amounts that were never yours, like refunds and marketplace-remitted sales tax) minus your costs, such as cost of goods sold, platform fees, and shipping you paid. This worksheet estimates that net figure; your own records and your tax preparer confirm it.

I sell on more than one platform and got more than one 1099-K — do I add them together?

Generally your total gross receipts across all platforms and payment methods count toward your business income, whether or not each individual platform issued a 1099-K. This worksheet lets you enter every platform's 1099-K as its own row and totals the reconciled result across all of them, so you have one combined figure instead of several separate ones.

Is this worksheet tax advice or a substitute for filing?

No. It performs arithmetic on the numbers you enter — it does not know your other income, does not determine your actual tax liability, and does not file anything with the IRS or any platform. Verify every figure against the platform's own 1099-K and payout statements, and treat the result as a worksheet for your own records or your tax preparer, not a conclusion.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. “Copy share link” encodes your rows into this page's own URL fragment rather than sending them anywhere — the fragment is never included in any network request, so nothing leaves your browser when you share it. vs-spreadsheet-comparison.html.text:
← 1099-K Reconciliation Worksheet

This worksheet vs. reconciling 1099-Ks yourself in a spreadsheet

The arithmetic is the same either way: Box 1a, minus refunds and marketplace-remitted sales tax, minus your costs, equals estimated net profit. The difference is whether that structure already exists when you sit down with two or three 1099-Ks in January, or whether you build it from scratch and hope you remembered both adjustments for every platform.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can produce exactly the same reconciled figure as this worksheet — subtracting refunds, marketplace-remitted sales tax, fees, cost of goods sold, and shipping from a gross figure is not exotic math. What a blank spreadsheet does not give you is a reminder that Box 1a includes two specific things that were never your income, or a place that already applies the same two adjustments identically across every platform's 1099-K instead of however carefully each row happened to be built that year.

This worksheet is that structure already built, with a built-in finding whenever the non-income adjustments look unusually large relative to Box 1a — the case a from-scratch spreadsheet is most likely to miss because nothing prompts for it.

QuestionWhere to answer it

Is this my final tax liability?Neither. Both stop at an estimate; your tax preparer confirms it.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your figures stay on this device.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't a spreadsheet just as accurate as this worksheet?

A correctly built one is — the arithmetic is Box 1a minus refunds minus marketplace-remitted sales tax minus your costs, which is ordinary subtraction. The risk is not the math, it is remembering that Box 1a includes sales tax you never kept and refunds you already gave back, and backing both out consistently across every 1099-K you received, often months after the sales happened and without the platform breaking either figure out clearly on the form itself.

When is a spreadsheet actually the better choice?

When your situation has a wrinkle this worksheet does not model — a marketplace that reports in a currency other than dollars, a platform that already nets refunds into Box 1a itself so backing them out again would double-count, or business income from outside any of these platforms entirely. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This worksheet trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for the common case: one or more marketplace 1099-Ks, each needing the same two non-income adjustments backed out.

What does a blank spreadsheet not remind you to do that this worksheet does?

Back out marketplace-remitted sales tax as its own line, separate from refunds. It is easy to remember refunds — you know which sales came back — and easy to forget that a chunk of Box 1a was never your money at all because the marketplace collected and paid the sales tax on your behalf. A spreadsheet built from scratch has no built-in prompt for that second adjustment; this worksheet raises a specific finding whenever the two adjustments together are an unusually large share of Box 1a, which is exactly the case a rushed spreadsheet is most likely to under-subtract.

Does this replace my tax preparer or a filed return?

No, and it is not built to. This worksheet and a spreadsheet both stop at estimating net profit from the 1099-K figures you supply — neither one knows your other income, your filing status, or your actual tax liability. That determination still belongs to you and, if you use one, your tax preparer, working from verified figures rather than either tool's estimate.

Open the reconciliation worksheet, or see why the gap between Box 1a and your actual income exists.

why-is-my-1099-k-higher-than-what-i-actu.text:
← Back to the 1099-K reconciliation worksheet

Why is your 1099-K higher than what you actually made?

Every filing season, resellers and gig-marketplace sellers open a Form 1099-K and don't recognize the number in Box 1a — it's often thousands of dollars more than what actually landed in their bank account after fees, refunds, and taxes. That gap is not a mistake on the form. It's how Box 1a is defined.

What Box 1a actually is

The IRS's own General Instructions for Forms 1099-K describe Box 1a as the gross amount of reportable payment-card and third-party network transactions for the year — reported "without regard to any adjustments for credits, cash equivalents, discounts, fees, refunds, or other amounts." In plain terms: it's the total dollar value of what moved through the platform's payment system tied to your account, before anything is subtracted.

Two specific things that inflate it

Sales tax the marketplace collected and remitted for you. Under marketplace-facilitator laws now in effect everywhere that levies sales tax, a large marketplace calculates, collects, and pays over sales tax on a seller's behalf automatically — the seller never sees that money and has no filing obligation for it. But the tax is still part of what the buyer paid, so it commonly counts toward Box 1a's gross total anyway.

Refunds. Because Box 1a is defined without regard to refunds, a sale you later refunded in full can still be counted in the gross figure, even though the buyer got their money back.

Neither of these is your income. Both need to be backed out before the number means anything about what you actually made.

What to actually do with it

  1. Pull the Box 1a total from each 1099-K you received.
  2. For each one, find (from the platform's own payout or tax summary, not a guess) how much of that total was refunds and how much was sales tax the platform remitted for you.
  3. Subtract your real costs — cost of goods sold, platform fees, shipping you paid — from what's left.
  4. What remains is your estimated net profit from that platform — the figure that actually belongs in a profit-and-loss calculation, not Box 1a itself.

The 1099-K reconciliation worksheet does exactly this arithmetic — for one platform or several at once — and exports the result as a CSV you can hand to whoever prepares your return.

Common questions

What does Form 1099-K Box 1a actually report?

The IRS's own General Instructions for Forms 1099-K define Box 1a as the gross amount of reportable payment transactions for the calendar year, "without regard to any adjustments for credits, cash equivalents, discounts, fees, refunds, or other amounts." It is the total dollar amount of transactions the platform processed for you, full stop — not a profit figure, and not even a figure net of money that was never yours to begin with.

Why would a platform include sales tax I never kept?

Under marketplace-facilitator laws now in effect in every state that levies sales tax, large marketplaces are required to calculate, collect, and remit sales tax on a seller's behalf — the seller never receives that money or has to file it themselves. But that tax is still part of the dollar amount the buyer paid and the platform processed, so it commonly ends up inside Box 1a's gross total. It was never the seller's income and does not belong in a profit calculation.

What about a refund I gave a buyer?

Box 1a is defined without regard to refunds, so a sale that was later refunded can still show up in the gross total even though the money went back to the buyer. Some platforms report refunds in a separate statement or a later box; not all break it out clearly on the 1099-K itself, which is exactly why it is worth reconciling by hand against your own payout history rather than assuming the form nets it out for you.
